assessment.nobel_worthiness: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene opened a new field: a theoretically predicted flat-band condition (continuum moire model) followed by experimental observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity in a clean, tunable carbon system. It is original, conceptually clear and has reshaped how electron correlation is studied in two-dimensional materials. It also speaks directly to my own interest in how band structure and interactions determine material properties.
assessment.attribution: The Bistritzer-MacDonald flat-band prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero group's 2018 experiments are the decisive pairing, so theory plus experiment fits a three-person prize. Experimental contributions from other groups and early twisted-graphene theory by others may be argued; I rely on the supplied credit only.
assessment.maturity: Strongly and independently reproduced by many groups within a few years, with a stable core interpretation of the flat bands and correlated states. Timing is arguably early, but the breadth of follow-on work is already large.
uncertainties: The microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated.
Other contributors to early moire and twisted-bilayer physics could challenge the credit allocation.
Whether the field has matured enough for a prize is a judgment call.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and the later giant effect in MgO barriers, made spintronic read heads and MRAM possible. It is a clear, magnetism-centred discovery with large technological and scientific impact, building on the already honoured GMR work.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera independently reported room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin's group developed the MgO junction (with the Yuasa/Djayaprawira work and Butler/Mathon-Umerski theory also part of the story). The three supplied names form a coherent set, but the MgO coherent-tunnelling part is shared with others not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Thoroughly confirmed, commercially deployed for over a decade, and with a stable physical interpretation (spin-dependent tunnelling, symmetry filtering). Recognition is timely or even somewhat overdue.
uncertainties: The credit boundary between the original TMR discovery and the MgO enhancement is unclear.
Important theory and parallel experimental contributions are not among the credited names.
A prize could be judged too close to the GMR prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators created a major branch of condensed-matter physics. The idea is original and clean, and it has been confirmed experimentally in several material systems with lasting impact on topological band theory and on electronic-structure approaches to topology.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele's theory is central; Molenkamp's HgTe experiments were decisive confirmation. Others, notably Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, and Moore, Balents, made key contributions, so the three-name set is a truncation of a wider history.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with broad independent experimental confirmation (HgTe, Bi-based materials, ARPES observations), though the 2016 prize already covered topological phases partly and the committee may see overlap.
uncertainties: Substantial credit competition among theorists, and one key contributor is deceased.
Overlap with the 2016 topological-phases prize may reduce appetite.
Practical applications remain limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Dynamical mean-field theory turned strongly correlated electrons from a conceptual problem into a quantitative computational framework, and with DFT+DMFT it connects to realistic materials. It has been widely adopted for Mott transitions, heavy fermions and transition-metal oxides. I know this method well and consider it a genuine, lasting theoretical-computational advance.
assessment.attribution: Credit is genuinely difficult: Metzner and Vollhardt's infinite-dimension limit, Mueller-Hartmann, and Georges and Kotliar's mapping to an impurity problem are each decisive, and the supplied names omit some of these. The three-person set is defensible but not clean.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with over three decades of use and comparison with experiment, though DMFT is an approximation whose accuracy is limited in low dimensions and its Nobel record in a theory-method category is uncertain.
uncertainties: Metzner and others are absent from the credited names, leaving the attribution incomplete.
A methods-and-computation prize is less typical than a discovery prize.
Predictive accuracy for real materials varies.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength proposal, achieved fractional uncertainties near the 10^-18 level and enable tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. The idea is original and the demonstrated precision is unmatched.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye developed the strontium clock to record accuracy. A two-person prize is clean, though other work on trapped-ion and lattice clocks exists (Ye's and Katori's groups, and others).
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed by multiple laboratories and in active use; the redefinition of the second is still pending, so timing could be argued either way.
uncertainties: Overlap with ion clocks and frequency-comb work already honoured.
Whether the redefinition of the second will strengthen the case or merely delay it.
Credit among other lattice-clock groups is not covered by the supplied names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum simulation with ultracold atoms in optical lattices (Mott insulator transition, Hubbard-model realisation, Fermi gases) created a controllable platform for many-body physics, bridging atomic and condensed-matter physics. It is conceptually clear and widely influential in understanding correlated systems.
assessment.attribution: Zoller and Jaksch provided the Bose-Hubbard proposal, Greiner and Bloch the Mott transition, and Esslinger the fermionic Hubbard work. With four credited names and the prize limited to three, some of these decisive contributors must be left out, which is an unresolved allocation problem.
assessment.maturity: Mature and independently reproduced, though the fully competitive simulation of open problems such as the 2D Hubbard model is still in progress. BEC prizes already recognised the underlying cooling.
uncertainties: Choosing three from four credited names leaves a real attribution gap.
Practical payoff versus classical simulation is not yet fully demonstrated.
Overlap with earlier BEC and cold-atom recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum anomalous Hall effect in magnetic topological insulators realised a quantised Hall conductance without an external field. It is an elegant joint magnetism and topology result and speaks to my interest in magnetically doped materials, though the experimental operating temperature remains very low.
assessment.attribution: Fang and Dai's theoretical prediction and Xue's group's experimental demonstration are the main pieces, but Haldane's model, Cui-Zu Chang's role in the first observation and related theory by others complicate the credit. Xue's experimental claim is the clearest of the three.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several groups, with a stable interpretation, but still at millikelvin to low-kelvin temperatures, which keeps it somewhat early and without applications.
uncertainties: Credit for the first observation versus the later groups needs scrutiny.
The very low operating temperature limits the practical significance.
Overlap with the 2016 topological prize and with Haldane's prior recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Event Horizon Telescope images of the M87* and Sgr A* shadows are first direct images of black-hole event horizons, with a very clear scientific and public impact and strong consistency with general relativity. They are a major measurement achievement, though they confirm rather than overturn expectations.
assessment.attribution: This is a large collaboration, so naming a few individuals is difficult. Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept and Doeleman led the VLBI effort and the collaboration build-up; Zensus's role is mainly institutional and leadership. A fair configuration is possible but inherently contested.
assessment.maturity: Recent but confirmed by two sources and by repeated epochs; the interpretation of the polarisation and spin is still developing. Recognition is plausible, but premature relative to the 2020 black-hole prize.
uncertainties: Collaboration credit is hard to allocate to individuals.
The recent timing and the 2020 black-hole prize may count against it.
Interpretation of the underlying astrophysical parameters is still evolving.
